headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from Continue’s filesystem/MCP access feeding LangGraph’s tool-driven orchestration.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read/write workspace files and use MCP, while LangGraph can execute developer-defined tools and persist graph state. If Continue ingests attacker-controlled file or MCP content and LangGraph treats it as instructions, the pair creates a direct instruction-smuggling path. Both profiles show shared filesystem/state channels, so the interaction is plausible by default.
conditions: IF Continue reads untrusted workspace content and forwards it into LangGraph nodes or tools
IF LangGraph nodes parse Continue output as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to all Continue outputs before LangGraph consumes them
Require a human review step for any tool-call text emitted by Continue
Restrict LangGraph nodes to a fixed schema for Continue-derived inputs
Disable MCP routes that can carry untrusted instructions
requires-engineering: implement content-sanitization and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers, and LangGraph can pass application-defined state through persistent checkpointers. If both are pointed at the same workspace or state store, sensitive code or secrets can flow from Continue into LangGraph outputs or logs. The pair is not proven to exfiltrate by default, but the shared-file/state pathway is real.
conditions: IF Continue and LangGraph share a workspace or checkpointer store
IF LangGraph logs or returns state containing editor-buffer contents
mitigations: Separate Continue workspace files from LangGraph state storage
Redact secrets before LangGraph persists or emits state
Limit Continue access to only the needed project directory
Review checkpointer retention settings before enabling shared runs
requires-engineering: add field-level redaction on graph state

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue has filesystem write access and broad network egress; LangGraph also has filesystem write, broad egress, and can spawn subprocesses and run browsers. Because LangGraph’s tools are developer-wired and Continue can operate on the same files, concurrent writes to shared mutable resources are plausible and can corrupt code or state. The profiles do not show locking, so conflict risk is high.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or checkpointer-backed state
IF LangGraph tools and Continue edits run concurrently without locks
mitigations: Run the agents on separate working directories
Serialize writes with a file or DB lock
Disable concurrent graph invocations during IDE editing
Use branch-per-agent workflows for code changes
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control to shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can generate code or instructions from editor context, and LangGraph can route that output into downstream tools or actions. If LangGraph treats Continue’s output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into tool execution, browser actions, or subprocesses. The pair therefore has a default path from generated text to action-taking authority.
conditions: IF LangGraph uses Continue output as node input without verification
IF downstream LangGraph nodes can execute shell, browser, or API actions
mitigations: Insert a verification node between Continue and any action-taking node
Require citations or structured outputs before execution
Cap LangGraph tools to read-only mode for initial runs
Log and diff Continue outputs before they trigger actions
requires-engineering: add policy gates for high-impact tool calls

E_compliance.rationale: Continue handles model-provider API keys and workspace files, while LangGraph can persist application state in external stores. If regulated data is present in the workspace or graph state, differing retention or residency settings can create compliance gaps. The profiles do not specify HIPAA/GDPR status, so I avoid stronger claims and choose medium due to the documented storage/egress surfaces.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in workspace files or graph state
IF the checkpointer or model provider stores data outside the required jurisdiction
mitigations: Confirm retention settings for both agents before use
Keep regulated data out of shared workspace files
Use a jurisdiction-approved checkpointer and model provider
Disable logging of prompts and graph state where possible
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing and retention controls
